solutions.check: grid and clues read from the FT's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Main heritage centre and railway terminus in Monaco, say

parts.note: main as an adjective means chief or principal

indicators.note: the centre of the word heritage is its middle pair of letters
a railway terminus is the end of the line, so the last letter of railway

explanation.surface: A tourist brochure praising the chief heritage centre and main railway station of Monaco.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centre' takes IT, the two middle letters of 'heritage'; 'terminus' takes Y, the last of 'railway'.
explanation.definitionFit: Monaco is ruled by a prince, an example of a state of that kind; 'say' marks it as one example.

clue.text: Two girls, perhaps, showing a bit of leg

parts.note: Pat is a girl's name
Ella is another girl's name

explanation.surface: A pair of girls showing a little leg.
explanation.definitionFit: The kneecap bone sits in the leg, so it is literally one small part of it.

clue.text: It's said to be good when one has had a long life

definitions.text: It's said to be good when one has had a long life

parts.words: It's said to be good when one has had a long life
parts.note: the saying 'he had a good ...' is used of someone who lived long, borrowing the cricket term for a batsman's turn at the crease

explanation.surface: A remark at a funeral about someone who lived a long time.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the batting turn is this word, and a long stay at the crease is 'a good' one; the phrase is a British idiom for a long life.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'had a good innings' praises a long life by comparing it to a long cricket batting turn.

clue.text: Flier is grumpy, getting request for payment

parts.note: grumpy means cross, bad-tempered
a bill is a written request for payment

explanation.surface: A pilot gets grumpy on receiving an invoice.
explanation.definitionFit: This finch is a bird, and birds are fliers.

clue.text: Turning up with old lady's cats

indicators.note: turning the little word up round makes it read backwards

parts.note: the old lady is slang for mother, ma, and the possessive gives an S

explanation.surface: An elderly woman's cats arriving on the scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning' reverses UP to PU; 'old lady' is informal for mother.
explanation.definitionFit: These are big American wild cats, so the plural noun is an example of cats.

clue.text: An Irish county, extremely large — it's on the border

indicators.note: extremely asks for the extreme letters, the first and last, of large

parts.note: the word it, with the 's read as 'is'
a rim is a border or edge

explanation.surface: A huge Irish county lying on the frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' picks LE, the outside letters of 'large'; the 's is the link 'is on'.
explanation.definitionFit: This is one of the counties of the Republic of Ireland, in Connacht, bordering Northern Ireland.

clue.text: Not running after bull in Spanish city

indicators.note: after places the scrambled letters after the bull

parts.note: the Spanish word for bull is toro

indicators.note: running as in a mixture or runny dye, signalling the letters of not are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man who is not taking part in a bull run in a Spanish city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running' rearranges NOT to NTO; the city is not Spanish at all, since 'in Spanish' belongs to the bull.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the largest city in Canada, capital of Ontario.

clue.text: Trace loose woman given complete freedom

indicators.note: loose means let free, so the letters of trace come undone and rearrange

parts.note: Blanche is a woman's name

explanation.surface: Tracking down a promiscuous woman who has been given total licence.
explanation.definitionFit: This French phrase, literally 'blank card', means full authority or unrestricted freedom to act.

clue.text: Merchant of Venice with a crazy notion

indicators.note: crazy means wild and disordered, signalling the letters of notion are jumbled

explanation.surface: A Venetian trader with a mad idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Merchant of Venice' looks like a description, but it names Shakespeare's title character; 'crazy' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's play The Merchant of Venice is named for this title character, the merchant who borrows from Shylock.

clue.text: In novel form, I'm great detective

indicators.note: novel means new, so putting the letters in a new form rearranges them

explanation.surface: A fictional sleuth boasting about himself in a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' pretends to mean a book, fitting a fictional detective, but it signals new order for IMGREAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Simenon's Inspector of the Paris police is a famous fictional detective.

clue.text: Unusual trees oft hewn in Hampshire?

indicators.note: unusual means out of the ordinary order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Odd how often trees are felled down in the Hampshire countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' rearranges TREESOFTHEWN. The definition is a description by example: something found in Hampshire, the question mark admitting it is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: This ancient woodland and national park lies in the south-western part of the English county of Hampshire.

clue.text: Stories about National Trust providing gifts

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the stories go round the trust's initials

parts.note: stories are tales
NT is the abbreviation for the National Trust, the British heritage charity

explanation.surface: Tales about the National Trust that make good presents.
explanation.definitionFit: Natural abilities are called gifts, a plural synonym.

clue.text: Odd compass used by leading characters in Star Trek

indicators.note: leading characters are the first letters of each word

parts.note: compass means scope or range

explanation.surface: A peculiar navigational instrument handled by the main cast of a sci-fi show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leading characters' looks like the stars of the show; it picks ST. The 'compass' is not the instrument but extent.
explanation.definitionFit: Odd and strange are synonyms meaning peculiar or unusual.

clue.text: Section of orchestra getting ready

definitions.meaning: the trumpets, trombones and horns make up this section

explanation.definitionFit: The orchestra's metal wind section shares its name with British slang for money, as does 'ready money'.

clue.text: Trouble at home with item of furniture

parts.note: in means at home
a commode is a chest of drawers or a chair hiding a chamber pot

explanation.surface: Problems at home involving a piece of furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: To inconvenience someone is to trouble them; both are verbs.

clue.text: Coach horse in accident losing tail

indicators.note: in puts the horse inside the shortened accident
losing its tail means the final letter drops off

parts.note: an accident in the sense of chance, luck
an Arab is a breed of horse

explanation.surface: A horse-drawn coach involved in a crash that cost the horse its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accident' means chance or luck, not a crash; 'losing tail' drops its final E before the horse goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an old-fashioned British word for a motor coach used for day trips.

clue.text: Almost entirely in one country or another

indicators.note: in places the shortened word inside the other country

parts.note: another country, here Austria

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter goes

parts.note: entirely means all

explanation.surface: Nearly everything takes place in one country or another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' cuts ALL to AL, which goes inside AUSTRIA; 'another' is a second country, so it stands for one.
explanation.definitionFit: This is one example of a country, the continent-sized nation in the southern hemisphere.

clue.text: Politician getting alliance to occupy half of Serbia

indicators.note: the alliance occupies, sits inside, the part of the country
half of a six-letter word is its first three letters

parts.note: NATO is the North Atlantic alliance

explanation.surface: A politician supports a military alliance occupying part of Serbia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half of' takes SER, the first three letters of 'Serbia'.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of a senate is a politician.

clue.text: Give new spirit to father — here's rum outside

indicators.note: outside means the scrambled letters go round the father
rum in British slang means odd, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of here's, the apostrophe ignored
Fr is the abbreviation for Father, a priest's title

explanation.surface: Revive Dad with a drink: here's some rum on the outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rum' looks like the drink, a spirit, but means strange in British slang and rearranges the letters of here's (REESH).
explanation.definitionFit: To refresh is to revive or reinvigorate, give new energy.

clue.text: Pig out? What's the matter?

definitions.meaning: pig out is to eat greedily, gorge oneself

explanation.definitionFit: Gorge oneself is one sense of the verb; material or substance is the noun's sense.

clue.text: Scots wear fancy aprons? That's about right!

indicators.note: about means around, so the rearranged letters go round the right
fancy means elaborate or fanciful, signalling the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Do Scotsmen wear decorative aprons? Close enough!
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' rearranges APRONS to SPORAN, placed round R.
explanation.definitionFit: This pouch worn in front of a kilt is a traditional item of Highland dress.

clue.text: In Paris a chance to play outside, down in the dumps

parts.note: un is French for a
hap is an old word for chance or luck

indicators.note: the outside letters of play, its first and last

explanation.surface: A French child gloomy at the chance to go out and play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' takes PY, the outer letters of 'play'.
explanation.definitionFit: Down in the dumps is an idiom meaning sad or depressed.

clue.text: Have a discussion about one tree

indicators.note: about places the discussion around the one

parts.note: to confer is to discuss
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Talking things over concerning a single tree.
explanation.definitionFit: A pine or fir is a cone-bearing tree of this kind.

clue.text: A girl sounding optimistic

indicators.note: sounding means as heard, so the word is said aloud

parts.note: a rosy outlook is an optimistic one

explanation.surface: A girl who sounds upbeat.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name used as an example of a girl; the clue's 'A girl' is a definition by example of a female forename.

clue.text: Someone else on a retreat to the bitter end

indicators.note: retreat means go back, so on a is read backwards
the end of bitter is its last letter

explanation.surface: Another person advancing then retreating right to the last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retreat' turns ON A into ANO; 'the bitter end' gives THE plus R, the last letter of 'bitter'.
explanation.definitionFit: Another means one more person or a different one, someone else.

clue.text: Part of class meets expectations, coming back for prizes

indicators.note: coming back means the run is read backwards
part of the phrase means a run of letters inside it

explanation.surface: Part of a class performing as hoped, returning for the awards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of' picks SMEETSE from 'claSS MEETS Expectations' and 'coming back' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: Prizes as a verb means values highly, the same as esteems.

clue.text: Relevant article by experts about post office

parts.note: a is the indefinite article

indicators.note: about places the experts around the post office

parts.note: pros are professionals, experts

explanation.surface: A relevant article written by experts about the post office.
explanation.definitionFit: Apropos means pertinent or to the point, a synonym of relevant.

clue.text: Roguish sweetheart held prisoner in clergyman's office

parts.note: arch means mischievous or roguish

indicators.note: held means the sweetheart holds the prisoner inside

parts.note: deary is a term of endearment, sweetheart
con is short for convict, a prisoner

explanation.surface: A scheming lover kept in jail inside a clergyman's office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roguish' suggests a villain but means arch, playfully mischievous; 'held' puts the prisoner inside the sweetheart.
explanation.definitionFit: The office or rank of a senior Anglican cleric below a bishop is this word.
